en: Advayavajra’s Works 9. *Sekatātparyasaṃgraha*,
edited by Mahāmahopādhyāya Haraprasad Shastri.
1. In *Advayavajrasaṃgraha*, GOS 1927, Baroda, edited by the Mikkyō Seiten Kenkyūkai; 2.
In the *Taishō Daigaku Sōgō Bukkyō Kenkyūjo Nenpō*.
*Taishō University Institute of Comprehensive Buddhist Studies Annual Report* 11, 1989, pp.
Homage to the Buddha!
Victorious is that certain one of great majesty, unfathomable, through the words of the spiritual friend.
He holds that reality which is beyond the reach of words, as if it were held in the palm of his hand.
Having understood the summary of the essential meaning of the initiations from various texts on initiation, we—Vajrācāryas possessing supreme knowledge—compose this according to the tradition. (2)
The first is the vase consecration; the second is the supreme secret;
the third is indeed the knowledge of wisdom; and the fourth is likewise that very same [knowledge]. (3)

The meaning of this is as follows: "First, the vase consecration (*kalaśābhiṣeka*). These are the six vase consecrations characterized by water, the crown, the vajra, the bell, and the master (*ācārya*). It is called a "consecration" (*seka*) because one is sprinkled (*sicyate*) with it for the purpose of washing away the stains of ignorance—the external impurity—just as with external water. All of these are designated as "vase consecrations" because they function through the vase. Furthermore, these six are irreversible consecrations because they have the nature of the Tathāgatas. For instance, the water consecration consists of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).

The nature of Akṣobhya is the crown consecration (*mukuṭābhiṣeka*), which consists of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) and has the nature of Ratnasaṃbhava. The vajra consecration (*vajrābhiṣeka*) consists of the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) and has the nature of Amitābha. The lordly consecration (*adhipatyābhiṣeka*) takes the form of all-accomplishing activity (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna*) and has the nature of Amoghasiddhi. The name consecration (*nāmābhiṣeka*)—due to the cessation of ignorance—is of the nature of the wisdom of the perfectly pure dharmadhātu accompanied by gnosis (*vidyā*), and is the very form of Vairocana. The master consecration (*ācāryābhiṣeka*), however, has the nature of Vajrasattva.
And here, the "five consecrations" refers to the *vidyā*-consecration, because the five *vidyās*, such as Locanā and the others, are active therein.

And here, for the sake of washing away the stains of ignorance, the water-consecration should be bestowed by the Vajrācārya in the form of Akṣobhya upon the disciple who takes Vairocana as his objective support. In this manner, the same identification (*ahaṃkāra*) applies everywhere.
The crown consecration is the seed of the future state of Buddhahood, which exists as the uṣṇīṣa within the mind.

By a measurement of twelve finger-breadths, [the central channel] is the *vajra* through its purity as the twelvefold dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). In its center is the syllable *HŪṂ*, which indicates the unsurpassed *dharmatā*. Its meaning is as follows: *ha* signifies being free from causes; *ū* signifies being devoid of conceptual construction (*ūha*); and *aṃ* signifies that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are non-abiding. From the opening of the lotus of existence (*bhavasaroja*), the Sages—whose forms consist of five spokes—radiate forth, having emerged from the body of existence through the purity of the five aggregates (*skandha*).

And here, by virtue of being oriented toward the center, it is indicated that all forms and so forth at the peripheries consist of consciousness. Furthermore, in order to demonstrate that all these are of the nature of everything, there is a square in every respect.

Then, those wise ones, having offered their own forms to the Dharma at Hūṃnāda, became liberated from the five [skandhas] and were manifested elsewhere at the periphery. For the sake of realizing emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), there is the threefold blossoming everywhere. These should be understood through the instruction of the Guru as consisting of the five wisdoms characterized by the mirror-like, the equality, the discerning, the performance of duties, and the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
And the collective meaning [of the term] indicates indestructible knowledge:
it is firm, essential, not fragile, and characterized by being uncuttable and indivisible.
Neither burning nor perishing, emptiness is called the vajra.
"In the *Hevajra*, it is said that 'the indestructible is the vajra.
And the purpose of this vajra-consecration is precisely to establish the seed of indestructible gnosis as it arises."

In the same way, the vajra-bell also—by virtue of its prior intention—is twelve finger-widths in measure; it represents the union of the downward-facing lotus and vajra in order to demonstrate that the nature of all phenomena is devoid of intrinsic existence (*niḥsvabhāva*). To awaken one to the fact that the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) is the cause of indivisible gnosis, there is a double garland of vajra-rows at the upper and lower parts. To proclaim that this [mandala] is a celestial palace whose nature is the three realms, there are various types of necklaces and half-necklaces. For this very reason, it is marked with the five Tathāgatas.

In order to indicate that the cause is the gnosis inseparable from emptiness and compassion (*śūnyatā-karuṇā*), there follows the exposition of the "Gate of Wisdom" (*prajñāmukha*). Furthermore, in order to explain that this gnosis, which is the very nature of the *dharmadhātu*, consists of the five Tathāgatas beginning with Vairocana, possesses the intrinsic nature of the five aggregates (*skandha*) such as form, and has the form of the five elements (*dhātu*) such as earth, the subsequent arrangement of the five spokes is presented. Here too, the orientation toward the spoke situated in the center and so forth is as previously described. Then, one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with this resounding vajra-bell, which grants authority over the awakening to all unsurpassed phenomena.

In this context, for the purpose of demonstrating preeminence and establishing the nature of the cause, the bestowal of the *vajrābhiṣeka* occurs first, even though the *vajraghaṇṭābhiṣeka* is the causal basis.

For the sake of demonstrating preeminence and establishing that all phenomena are merely names, as well as for the purpose of providing the introductory narrative (*nidāna-avadāna*) for the name appropriate to the future state of a Lord of Munis, the *nāmābhiṣeka* is performed by discarding the previous name in accordance with the family and lineage (*gotra*) of one’s own deity.

And the master initiation (*ācāryābhiṣeka*) is characterized by the commitments of the vajra, the commitments of the bell, the commitments of the mudrā, the authorization, the vows, the prophecy, and the consolation. From this point forward, the "vajra commitment" is for the purpose of awakening [the disciple] to the realization that "you are the commitment of awareness that carries the union of the unconditioned and the indivisible. The "bell commitment" is for the purpose of demonstrating that "you are the supreme among the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma. The "mudrā commitment" is for the purpose of proclaiming that "you are the very nature of one's chosen deity."

The reality of the maṇḍala, characterized by the purity of the maṇḍala; the reality of the deity, characterized by the purity of the deity; the preparation of the master; the knowledge for accomplishing the maṇḍala; the consumption of the five lamps and the five nectars as a sign of fitness; and their reality as the absence of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvabhāvya*) from the perspective of the completion stage (*utpannakrama*). [This constitutes] the authorization for the purpose of turning the wheel of Dharma.

The bestowal of the vajra-vow is for the purpose of abolishing external vows. The prophecy is for the purpose of indicating that [the disciple] has the nature of the elements, such as earth and so forth; for its meaning is: "May you become *bhūḥ* (earth), *bhuvaḥ* (atmosphere), and *svar* (heaven)," which signifies that the self-nature (*svaḥ*) of the ground (*bhūḥ*), the support (*dharā*), and so on, shall become [your own]. The encouragement is for the purpose of awakening [him] from this point forward, [saying]: "You are now liberated from all obscurations and equal to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."

The secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*) consists of the bestowal of the *bodhicitta* produced by both [the master and the consort] at the same time, for the purpose of making wisdom and faith into a field and for the purpose of guarding the commitments (*samaya*). Its etymological derivation is "that which causes [one] to give through the secrets of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*).
Regarding the term "wisdom-knowledge" (*prajñājñāna*), [it is as follows]:

There are two etymological derivations. First, *prajñā* is knowledge (*jñāna*), or *prajñā* itself is external knowledge. In that context, *prajñā* is the intellect (*buddhi*) which maintains the forms of the grasped and the grasper; it consists of the four elements and the five aggregates, has the six sense objects such as form as its nature, and has the woman as its essence. Knowledge of the *bodhicitta* is the knowledge of that [intellect] which serves as the causal sign—this is the first derivation. The second derivation is that when that very same [intellect] is empty of the two forms [of subject and object], it is consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Some maintain that the fourth meaning is the goal to be accomplished, endowed with the seven limbs characterized by the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*). Others hold that the fourth meaning is the knowledge of wisdom itself, when it has been cultivated until it resembles the stainless autumn sky. Still others maintain that the fourth meaning is the knowledge of wisdom itself, which is both primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and its transformation (*vikāra*), consisting of the arising of primordial nature, and possessing a perfectly pure intrinsic nature that flows as the non-duality of the "yoked-together" (*yuganaddha*). Other alternative positions are not stated here for fear of excessive prolixity.

By means of this verse endowed with merit, which is gathered from the ritual procedure for the collection of the most secret empowerments, may there be receptivity toward the pure and clear sublime teachings of the Sugata for the entire world. (4)
And thus this *Sekatātparya-saṃgraha* is completed.
This work is by the scholar-avadhūta, the venerable Śrī Advayavajra.
